name: Churches and Faith Organisations
blurb: Sermon prep, administration, and pastoral limits across hundreds of thousands of congregations, from Barna research and faith-tech platforms to Notre Dame ethics work.

points.desc: Census BTOS covers religious and civic organisations within its service-sector series; no better official measure exists yet, and this page says less rather than guessing.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The research firm's State of the Church work quantitatively tracks AI adoption, perception, and use among US congregations and ministry leaders - the closest thing to sector-wide survey data.
points.name: Barna Group runs the national studies

points.desc: Used by thousands of US churches, Gloo surveys faith leaders and builds AI tooling for ministry - a primary source for what deployment actually looks like in congregations.
points.name: Gloo is the sector's tech platform

points.desc: The interfaith nonprofit network brings scholars, technologists, and clergy together on the ethical deployment of AI in religious contexts.
points.name: AI and Faith convenes the ethics work

points.desc: The university's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good funds and tracks research on AI's impact on faith and religious life.
points.name: Notre Dame studies AI and human formation

points.desc: The Hartford Institute for Religion Research regularly surveys congregational trends and digital adoption across American places of worship.
points.name: Hartford surveys congregational technology

points.desc: Pew Research Center's Religion & Public Life work periodically measures how the public and clergy view technology and AI in religious spaces.
points.name: Pew measures public and clergy attitudes

summary: No single body tracks AI adoption across America's hundreds of thousands of congregations - coverage comes from research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes, and this page names them rather than pretending a census exists. Sermon research, translation, accessibility, and administration are the working uses; every tradition is writing its own guidance.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Business Outlook Survey places religious organizations within the broader Other Services category (NAICS 81), where 12.6% of firms reported using AI in the most recent period, up from 11.3% in the prior period. That figure covers a wide range of service businesses and is not specific to congregations alone, so it should be read as an approximate ceiling rather than a precise congregational adoption rate. No dedicated government survey isolates houses of worship, and the Hartford Institute for Religion Research, which has a 45-year history of tracking congregational trends and digital adoption, represents one of the few organizations positioned to eventually fill that gap with sector-specific data.

Among the uses that have drawn the most attention, sermon preparation stands out as both the most visible application and the most contested. Per Notre Dame, a University of Notre Dame professor of philosophy leading research on AI and religion has stated that using AI to draft anything spoken in worship reflects a basic misunderstanding of what Christians believe is happening when a preacher delivers a homily. The Barna Group's research reinforces that tension from the pew side, finding that nearly all pastors worry AI could misread scripture, and that most want AI to present every interpretation of a difficult passage rather than settle on one. These findings suggest that even where AI tools are adopted for content work, clergy and congregants are drawing careful lines around authority and interpretation.

On the infrastructure side, Gloo positions itself as the primary technology platform for faith-based organizations in the United States, describing an AI offering that includes values-aligned models, developer tools, and benchmarks built specifically for missional leaders. The platform supports inference, retrieval-augmented generation, and assistant workflows, and frames its tooling around what it calls a comprehensive evaluation framework measuring AI alignment across seven research-backed dimensions of human flourishing. Gloo's approach to ministry workflows, data unification, and knowledge graphs points toward administrative and organizational intelligence as a significant near-term deployment category, even if preaching remains sensitive territory.

The ethics conversation around AI in religious contexts is organized and growing. AI and Faith, an interfaith nonprofit, describes its mission as equipping people of faith to bring time-tested, faith-based values to the ethical AI conversation, and frames issues of control, privacy, bias, economic well-being, and human identity as inherently moral and, for the 85 percent of the world's population who claim a religious affiliation, deeply spiritual. The organization seeks to inject humility and historicity into an industry that has often rejected both, connecting technologists, theologians, and ethicists. Notre Dame's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good similarly funds interdisciplinary work on AI and religion, with a focus on practical models for ethical technology design and deployment.

For a decision-maker at a congregation or faith-based organization weighing whether to deploy AI, the evidence suggests the technology is arriving whether or not institutions plan for it, and that the organizations most likely to navigate it well are those treating ethical alignment as a design requirement rather than an afterthought. Administrative uses, data integration, and workflow automation carry less theological risk than content generation for worship, and platforms like Gloo have begun building sector-specific guardrails to address values alignment. Pew Research Center's ongoing measurement of clergy and public attitudes toward technology in religious spaces will be worth watching as a barometer of where congregational tolerance for AI actually lands over time.
